\chapter{Permission, Notice, and the Word}
\label{ch:permiso-y-voz}
\hlchaptermodality{332}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say el permiso, el aviso, la disculpa, la palabra and la voz, and say which Greek geometry term became the Spanish word for word.}

Complete ES-C332-voz: open the noun inside con permiso, give an aviso, offer a disculpa, and carry a palabra on your voz.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el permiso]{el permiso — the noun you have been saying since \emph{con permiso}}

\label{lesson:ES-C332-permiso}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the thing}, then \emph{the matter}. (\emph{La cosa}; \emph{el asunto}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item con permiso — the phrase this word already lives in.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{per-MI-so}, three beats with the weight in the middle. The \emph{r} is a single tap, and the \emph{s} stays crisp all the way to the end. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el permiso} — \textquotedblleft{}permission,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}leave,\textquotedblright{} and on paper, \textquotedblleft{}a permit.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{mittere} meant \emph{to send, to let go}. Put \textbf{per-} in front — \emph{through} — and \textbf{permittere} is \emph{to let go through}. Its past participle \textbf{permissus} is \emph{let through}, and that is where this noun comes from.

That is a nicer picture than the English word gives you. To grant permission is not to approve; it is to \textbf{stand out of the way}. You were going somewhere, and somebody let you through.

Which is exactly what \textbf{con permiso} does. You have been saying it to squeeze past people in a corridor — \emph{with permission} — and the word inside it means \emph{with being-let-through}. The phrase and its literal sense agree perfectly.

\emph{Mittere} is one of the busiest roots in English, and once you hear the \emph{-mit-} and \emph{-miss-} you will hear it everywhere. To \textbf{permit} is to send through. To \textbf{transmit} is to send across. To \textbf{submit} is to send under. To \textbf{admit} is to send toward. To \textbf{dismiss} is to send away. To \textbf{emit} is to send out. A \textbf{missile} is a thing sent, a \textbf{mission} is a sending, and a \textbf{missionary} is somebody sent.

Even \textbf{promise} belongs: \emph{prō mittere}, to send forth — words sent ahead of the deed they commit you to.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five words for what courtesy is actually made of. \emph{Por favor} gave you \emph{el favor}; now \emph{con permiso} gives you this.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el permiso}
  \item \emph{con permiso}
  \item \emph{un permiso más}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{mittere} mean? (To send, to let go.) And what does \emph{permittere} mean piece by piece? (To let go through.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el aviso]{el aviso — a notice is something made to be seen}

\label{lesson:ES-C332-aviso}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the matter}, then \emph{permission}. (\emph{El asunto}; \emph{el permiso}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el permiso — the word you met one lesson ago.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{a-VI-so}, three beats, the weight in the middle. The \emph{v} is soft, made without the lips closing fully. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el aviso} — \textquotedblleft{}the notice,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the warning,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the heads-up.\textquotedblright{}

Behind it is the verb \textbf{avisar}, \emph{to notify}, and behind that is Latin \textbf{ad vīsum} — \emph{toward what has been seen}. The root verb is \textbf{vidēre}, \emph{to see}.

So an \emph{aviso} is not an instruction. It is a \textbf{making-visible}: somebody has put a thing where you can see it, and what you do next is yours to decide. That is why \emph{aviso} covers a posted notice, a warning sign and a friendly heads-up without straining.

English built two words on the identical formation. \textbf{Advise} and \textbf{advice} come from the same \emph{ad vīsum} through French, and they carry the same modesty — to advise is to make something visible to somebody, not to command them.

\emph{Vidēre} is one of the great English suppliers. \textbf{Vision} and \textbf{visible} and \textbf{visit} are obvious. \textbf{Evident} is \emph{ē-vidēns}, seeing-out, plain to see. To \textbf{provide} is to see beforehand, and \textbf{prudent} is the same word worn down. \textbf{Survey} is to see over. A \textbf{video} is, in Latin, the single word \emph{I see}. And \textbf{envy} is \emph{invidia}, seeing against — looking at somebody with a bad eye.

Spanish uses the phrase \textbf{sin previo aviso}, \emph{without prior notice}, and you now have both halves of the idea.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two of five. A word for being let through, and a word for being shown.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el aviso}
  \item \emph{un aviso}
  \item \emph{sin aviso}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{vidēre} mean? (To see.) And which two English words come from the same \emph{ad vīsum}? (\emph{Advise} and \emph{advice}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la disculpa]{la disculpa — an apology is blame taken back off}

\label{lesson:ES-C332-disculpa}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{permission}, then \emph{the notice}. (\emph{El permiso}; \emph{el aviso}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la culpa — the noun this word undoes.
  \item perdón — the apology you already say.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dis-CUL-pa}, three beats with the weight in the middle. The \emph{c} before \emph{u} is a hard \emph{k}, and the \emph{l} is light and forward. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la disculpa} — \textquotedblleft{}the apology,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the excuse.\textquotedblright{}

This one is transparent once the seam is named. \textbf{Dis-} is the Latin prefix that undoes, reverses or removes. \textbf{Culpa} is Latin for \emph{fault, blame}. So a \emph{disculpa} is, structurally, \textbf{an un-blaming} — the act of taking the fault back off somebody.

You already have the second half on its own: \textbf{la culpa} is blame, and \emph{es mi culpa} is \emph{it is my fault}.

English kept \emph{culpa} without ever building the negative form. Somebody \textbf{culpable} is blameworthy. A \textbf{culprit} is the one who carries the blame. To \textbf{exculpate} is to clear of blame — \emph{ex-culpa}, blame out — which is the same idea as \emph{disculpa} built with a different prefix. And \textbf{mea culpa} is Latin still being spoken, word for word: \emph{my fault}.

There is a difference in feel worth having. \textbf{Perdón} asks the other person to give something — pardon, a gift of forgiveness. \textbf{Disculpa} does the work at your own end: you are removing the blame yourself. And \textbf{disculpe} is the polite form you use to stop a stranger, where English says \emph{excuse me} — which is, note, the same idea again, blame removed from \emph{me}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three of five. Let through, shown, and un-blamed.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la disculpa}
  \item \emph{una disculpa}
  \item \emph{sin disculpa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the \emph{dis-} in \emph{disculpa} do? (It undoes — it removes the blame.) And what does \emph{mea culpa} mean word for word? (My fault.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la palabra]{la palabra — a word that is Greek for \emph{thrown alongside}}

\label{lesson:ES-C332-palabra}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the notice}, then \emph{the apology}. (\emph{El aviso}; \emph{la disculpa}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la voz — the sound a word is carried on, next lesson.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pa-LA-bra}, three beats with the weight in the middle. The \emph{b} between vowels is soft, made without the lips fully meeting, and \emph{br} runs together as one cluster. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la palabra} — \textquotedblleft{}the word.\textquotedblright{}

Latin had a perfectly good word for \emph{word}: \textbf{verbum}. Spanish barely uses its descendant. What it uses instead is a borrowed Greek technical term that got loose.

Greek \textbf{parabol\'{\={e}}} meant \emph{a throwing beside} — \textbf{para-} (beside) plus \textbf{bállein} (to throw). It named a \textbf{comparison}: you throw one thing down next to another so the likeness shows. Greek-speaking writers used it for a figure of speech, and the Latin Bible took it over as \textbf{parabola} for the comparison-stories Jesus told.

Those stories were so central to preaching that the word for them drifted outward — from \emph{the comparison} to \emph{the speech} to \emph{the utterance} to, finally, \emph{the single word}. Spanish smoothed \textbf{parabola} into \textbf{palabra}, swapping the \emph{r} and \emph{l} along the way, and ended up with its ordinary noun.

Meanwhile the untouched Greek form was borrowed a second time, and English has both. A \textbf{parable} is the story. A \textbf{parabola} is the curve, named because it lies alongside a line of the cone. \textbf{Parley} is talk, \textbf{parole} is a prisoner released on his word, and \textbf{Parliament} is the place where the talking happens.

Latin \emph{verbum} did survive in Spanish, but only in the grammatical \textbf{verbo} — and in English \textbf{verb}, \textbf{verbal} and \textbf{proverb}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four of five. And one of them turns out to be a Greek geometry term that went to church.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la palabra}
  \item \emph{otra palabra}
  \item \emph{una palabra más}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Greek \emph{parabol\'{\={e}}} mean? (A throwing beside — a comparison.) And which Latin word did \emph{palabra} push out of everyday use? (\emph{Verbum}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la voz]{la voz — the voice, and the vowels named after it}

\label{lesson:ES-C332-voz}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the apology}, then \emph{the word}. (\emph{La disculpa}; \emph{la palabra}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la palabra — what this one carries.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{VOS}, one beat. The \emph{v} is soft. The final \emph{z} is a plain \emph{s} across the Americas, and a \emph{th} sound in much of Spain. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la voz} — \textquotedblleft{}the voice.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{vōx}, in its other cases \textbf{vōcem}, which is the form Spanish worked from — that is why the \emph{c} shows up in every relative and the \emph{z} only here.

English took the word twice, once through French and once from Latin directly, which is why the family looks slightly mixed. \textbf{Voice} came through French. \textbf{Vocal}, \textbf{vocalise}, \textbf{vociferous} and \textbf{vocabulary} came straight from the books.

A \textbf{vowel} is the quiet surprise in the list. It is \emph{vocālis littera} — \emph{the vocal letter}, the one made with voice alone and nothing blocking it. Every other letter needs some obstruction; a vowel is pure voice. The name is a definition.

A \textbf{vocation} is a \emph{calling} — the noun assumes somebody is doing the calling. An \textbf{advocate} is one called to your side, which is what a lawyer is. To \textbf{evoke} is to call out, to \textbf{provoke} is to call forth, to \textbf{revoke} is to call back, and to \textbf{convoke} is to call together.

Spanish has \textbf{en voz alta} — \emph{in a high voice}, meaning \emph{aloud} — and its partner \textbf{en voz baja}, under your breath.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five words for the machinery of politeness and speech: \emph{el permiso}, \emph{el aviso}, \emph{la disculpa}, \emph{la palabra}, \emph{la voz}. Two of them were inside phrases you already said.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la voz}
  \item \emph{mi voz}
  \item \emph{una voz más}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is a \textbf{vowel}, translated from its Latin name? (A vocal letter — made with voice alone.) And what is an \textbf{advocate}? (One called to your side.)
\end{tcolorbox}
